summary: Presents a framework for large-scale measurement of broadband performance. It describes the logical architecture, the components and their interactions, and defines terminology for LMAP.

eli5.summary: A plan for putting many little speed-testers in many homes, with a central manager.

subtitle: An architecture for letting one organisation run broadband tests on huge numbers of devices and collect the results.

tldr.problem: Operators and regulators want to run the same broadband measurements across hundreds of thousands or millions of devices, but existing systems are proprietary and reach only up to a few thousand agents.
tldr.mechanism: The LMAP framework splits a measurement system into Measurement Agents that run tasks, Controllers that send them Instructions, and Collectors that receive Reports, linked by a Control Protocol and a Report Protocol over secure channels.
tldr.outcome: It defines the terminology, the protocol model and the deployment, security and privacy considerations, while leaving the actual protocols, metrics and bootstrap mechanisms to other specifications.

facts.label: Expected scale
facts.value: A few hundred thousand or millions of MAs

facts.label: Controllers per MA
facts.value: One at any point in time

sections.title: Goals of the Framework
sections.content:
The Large-Scale Measurement of Broadband Performance (LMAP) framework coordinates broadband measurements and result collection across many Measurement Agents (MAs). An MA may be software on a PC, an embedded agent in a consumer device or home gateway, a dedicated probe, or a function on an ISP device such as a DSLAM or Carrier Grade NAT. A system could easily encompass a few hundred thousand or even millions of MAs.

Use cases include operators planning networks and finding faults, and regulators benchmarking operators. The design goals are that a system be standardised, large-scale, diverse (agents from different vendors, wired or wireless, IPv4 or IPv6) and privacy respecting. The RFC notes that existing systems are proprietary in some or all aspects and have up to a few thousand MAs.
sections.eli5: The goal is one shared way to run the same speed tests in millions of homes, and to keep people's private information safe while doing it.

sections.title: Components and Terminology
sections.content:
Three elements form the core. The Measurement Agent initiates Measurement Tasks. The Controller tells MAs what tasks to perform and when (the Measurement Schedule) and how to report (the Report Schedule). The Collector accepts Reports containing the Measurement Results and passes them to a repository.

A Measurement Method defines how to measure a Metric. Some methods only observe existing traffic (an Observed Traffic Flow). Others create Measurement Traffic and need a partner: a Measurement Peer (MP), which helps the MA but is not managed by the Controller, or a second MA. The RFC's example is an MA sending an ICMP echo request to a responder. The Control Channel carries Instructions and Capabilities, Failure and Logging Information; the Report Channel carries Reports.

Outside the initial scope are the bootstrapper, a subscriber parameter database (for example whether a contract is 2, 40 or 80 Mb/s, since a test for an 80 Mb/s line may overwhelm a 2 Mb/s line), data analysis tools and a results repository.

Two constraints apply: the Measurement System is under the direction of a single organisation, and each MA has only one Controller at any point in time, which spares MAs from resolving conflicting schedules.
sections.eli5: There is a boss who gives out jobs, helpers who do the tests, and one mailbox where the answers go. Each helper only listens to one boss at a time.

sections.title: Protocol Model: Control, Tasks and Reports
sections.content:
An LMAP system goes through bootstrapping, the Control Protocol, the Measurement Tasks themselves, and the Report Protocol. Bootstrapping gives the MA its identifier (an MA-ID, a device identifier, or both), an optional Group-ID and its Control Channel details. LMAP does not define a bootstrap mechanism, since it depends on the device and access.

With the Control Protocol the Controller sends an Instruction: the Measurement Task configurations (a Metric given as a URI to a registry entry, Input Parameters, optional interface and Cycle-ID), the Schedules, the Report Channel and any Suppression information. Suppression temporarily stops tasks or reports, for example when there is an unexpected network issue, and an Un-suppress message ends it. The Control Protocol does not let the MA negotiate. The MA reports its Capabilities, Failure and Logging Information, and after a reboot should pause for a random delay, perhaps about one minute, to avoid a mass calling event.

Once instructed, the MA acts autonomously. It may run pre-checks, such as confirming there is no cross-traffic, and can be given a time limit after which it stops tasks if it hears nothing from the Controller. The Report contains the MA-ID or Group-ID, the results with times, the task details, the Cycle-ID and optionally the subscriber's service parameters. The RFC suggests that the underlying transfer could be push, pull or hybrid, such as REST-style HTTP(S), or NETCONF-YANG and IPFIX.
sections.eli5: The boss sends a to-do list with a schedule. The helper does the tests on its own, then mails the results. If there is trouble, the boss can tell all helpers to pause.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The Controller should know each MA's capabilities and keep schedules sensible, avoid harming the end user (including any effect on a subscriber's bill or traffic cap), and think carefully about how to interpret missing results. A system may have several Controllers, for example for different device types, locations or load balancing.

An MA can sit on a networked device such as a smartphone or laptop, in a site gateway, behind a NAT or firewall, on a multihomed device, or inside an ISP network. A gateway is described as one of the better places, since all site-to-ISP traffic passes through it. Behind a NAT or firewall the Controller may not be able to reach the MA unless port forwarding or pin holing is set up, for example by the MA sending keepalives. On a multihomed device the Instruction can name which interface to measure, and the result should include the network measured.

Examples of Measurement Peers include a web server used for a speed test, a TWAMP server and Session-Reflector, an OWAMP server, and each router that answers in a traceroute-like measurement. A one-way test can also use two MAs, one sending and one measuring.
sections.eli5: The little tester can live in a phone, a home router, or inside the internet company's own equipment. Where it lives changes how the boss can reach it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Instructions must be authenticated, checked for integrity and not vulnerable to replay attacks. A malicious party controlling an MA could launch denial-of-service attacks, create a platform for pervasive monitoring, reduce user experience or corrupt results. Instruction Messages need encryption, and reports must be encrypted, authenticated and protected from tampering.

Collectors are contacted repeatedly, so they should limit connections, transmission rate and storage per MA, and quickly reject unknown sources. Data from customer-controlled devices is to some degree inherently untrustworthy, so an operator should be cautious about relying on results for action such as refunding fees under a service level agreement. The RFC also mentions the risk of "gaming the system": a regulator benchmarking operators could be fooled if an operator identifies and prioritises the measured lines, which it treats as a code-of-conduct matter outside the initial scope.
sections.eli5: Only the real boss should be able to give orders, and only the real mailbox should get the answers, so nobody can fake either one.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC treats privacy as a core requirement: by default the Control and Report Protocols should operate in a privacy-sensitive manner. It identifies individual users, ISPs, regulators and other LMAP operators as entities with sensitive information. Examples include MAC addresses, IP addresses, location, subscribed service parameters, traffic contents, and for ISPs the measurement instructions, schedules and network topology.

Mitigations discussed include data minimisation (less detail for general reporting than for troubleshooting), anonymity through measurement point designations such as mp000 instead of IP addresses or by reporting a Group-ID instead of an MA-ID, pseudonymity (with the caveat that long-term use weakens it), and obtaining the subscriber's informed consent. The RFC says anonymization of network trace data on its own is insufficient for many data protection applications.
sections.eli5: Test results should not reveal who you are or where you live. Using a group name instead of your own name helps hide you in the crowd.

items.title: Standardised
items.text: Tasks, components, data models and protocols, so results are comparable.

items.title: Large-scale
items.text: A few hundred thousand or even millions of agents.

items.title: Diversity
items.text: Agents from different vendors, networks and address families.

items.title: Privacy respecting
items.text: Protocols and procedures respect everyone's sensitive information.
